newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU ministers to finalise details of EMU budget pact.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers to finalise details of EMU budget pact.

text.p: A European Union pact designed to curb excessive government spending under a single currency will be scrutinised of EU finance ministers and central bankers meeting this weekend in the Netherlands.
While the central elements of the Stability and Growth Pact were agreed by EU leaders in Dublin last December, a few loose ends need to clarified before the accord can become law.
In broad terms, the Dublin pact comprises three areas:
-- an early warning system designed to detect any slippages in government finances;
-- a tightening of the Maastricht treaty's excessive deficit procedure, including a clarification of potential sanctions;
-- a regulation that seeks to give EU finance ministers guidance in imposing penalties on governments with annual deficits over three percent of gross domestic product.
Should an excessive deficit occur, the offending government will have at least two years to correct the overshoot or face sanctions, initially in the form of a non-interest-bearing deposit.

The fines contain a fixed -- 0.2 percent of GDP -- and variable component -- equal to one tenth of the excess of the deficit over the three percent target. A maximum penalty of 0.5 percent of output was also agreed.
Where there is still disagreement is on whether the fines should be cumulative.
For example, if a government was penalised for a given year and failed to correct it within the specified time frame, would it be fined again, essentially making the penalties cumulative.
Some EU governments believe such an approach would be too severe, particularly if a country faced the maximum penalty.
Others see a cumulative system as the most effective way of encouraging budgetary rigour.

Another unresolved issue is the amount of discretion EU finance minsiters should have in determining whether a country indeed has a deficit overshoot. This is a very legalistic point and revolves around the wording of the pact.
The proposed regulation says EU ministers would "as a rule, decide to impose sanctions" if a country failed to rectify its deficit problem.
Some governments argue that where there is a rule there is an exception and that such language weakens the automatic nature of the process, a concern very much shared by Germany.
"I would say that nobody really questions the need for a stringent system, but some say there should be this element of discretion," said one EU diplomat.
Only by including such discretion would the pact be in line with the principles of the Maastricht treaty, an argument many EU countries have made, say diplomats.
One last point is how to distribute the fines -- in other words should the money benefit only those within the EMU area or should it be dispersed more widely to include all 15 EU nations.

On all of these points diplomats said the expectation is that they will not cause any considerable difficulties and would be resolved in time for EU leaders to endorse when they meet in Amsterdam in June.
